newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's northwest plants no soybeans this season.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's northwest plants no soybeans this season.

text.p: Mexico's northwest planted no soybeans this season because of a water shortage at the crucial plantings period, the local office of the American Soybean Association (ASA) said Tuesday.

Citing soybean crushers from the states of Sinaloa and Sonora, the ASA said they confirmed no plantings had been made and all their beans currently being crushed were being imported from the United States.
"All bean imports for that region cross the border at Nogales, in Arizona although some crushers have imported boatloads through the port of Manzanillo," the ASA said in a statement.
"Some crushers in the northwest predict that soybeans will be planted in the region again in the summer/fall season next year (for autumn/winter harvesting)," the local office said.

"The principle criteria is that there is now enough water for irrigation in Sinaloa and Sonora for the next two years. Our expectation is that soybean hectarage in the northwest will be minimal next year, probably not exceeding 15,000 hectares," the ASA added.

Drought ravaged northern Mexico for two years until this summer when rains, aided by a wave of hurricanes and tropical storms, brought relief to most of the states that border the United States, filling up local reservoirs as well.
Mexico's northwest has traditionally been the number two area of the country for soybeans.

The top producer state is Tamaulipas in the northeast, but even that state has seen local output suffer in recent years, with the ASA only estimating 6,000 hectares planted in southern Tamaulipas this season.
--Chris Aspin, Mexico City newsroom (525) 7289530. E-mail at chris.aspin@reuters.com
